query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys that incorporate a sufficient amount of reactive elements (such as Al, Ti, or Cr) develop a continuous, adherent oxide layer (for example, a spinel phase) at high temperatures because these elements preferentially oxidize. The formed oxide acts as a self-healing barrier, significantly reducing further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a multiphase microstructure synthesized from uniformly mixed elemental or powder precursors containing reactive elements (e.g., Al, Ti, Cr) in amounts designed to favor selective oxidation.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to elevated temperatures (around 800–900 °C) in an oxidative (air) atmosphere for a fixed duration, while also preparing a control alloy with a deliberately reduced concentration of the reactive elements.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation tests conducted in air for durations on the order of hours (e.g., 20 hours at 800–900 °C) to allow oxide layer formation and stabilization.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent oxide film—identified as a spinel phase or similar stable oxide—that forms preferentially along regions enriched with reactive elements.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the reactive elements oxidize more readily than the other constituents, leading to the formation of a self-healing oxide film. This film retards further diffusion of oxygen into the bulk alloy, thereby significantly lowering the rate of oxidation compared to alloys lacking sufficient reactive element content.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys containing higher levels of reactive elements will form a more uniform, dense, and adherent oxide layer. This should manifest as reduced oxidation weight gain (or lower parabolic oxidation rate constants) and improved surface integrity (e.g., fewer spallation events) relative to a baseline alloy with a lower reactive element concentration.
generation.baseline: A similar high-entropy alloy with only minimal amounts of reactive elements, expected to exhibit discontinuous or non-protective oxide layer formation and higher overall oxidation rates under the same testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies primarily under high-temperature oxidative conditions (approximately 800–900 °C) and over time periods sufficient for oxide layer growth (e.g., several hours). It may not be valid for lower temperature exposures or extremely high temperatures where spallation or different degradation modes predominate.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of reactive element content in promoting adherent oxide formation is supported by analogous systems, the quantitative extent of oxidation rate reduction and the self-healing efficacy require further experimental validation under controlled processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with identical processing: one set enriched with higher levels of reactive elements (e.g., increased Al/Ti/Cr) and one control set with lower reactive element content. Expose both sets to 800–900 °C in air for 20 hours. Post-exposure, characterize the surface and cross-sectional oxide layer morphology using SEM and XRD, and measure the oxidation weight gain per unit area.
measurements: XRD phase analysis to identify and quantify the protective oxide (e.g., spinel) phase
SEM imaging of the oxide layer for continuity and adhesion assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reactive element–enriched samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain or do not form a continuous, adherent oxide layer compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
